body.text: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has declared himself a ‘pacemaker’ for peace in actively pursuing a policy of conciliation with North Korea. But Dongwook Kim writes the policy instead looks like appeasement of an increasingly bellicose regime that risks undermining South Korean security.

The inauguration of President Lee Jae-myung of the liberal Democratic Party on 4 June 2025, following the ousting of President Yoon Suk-yeol of the conservative People Power Party, marked the start of an about-face in South Korea’s policy towards North Korea.

The Lee government has revived the Democratic Party’s longstanding dialogue-oriented and conciliatory approach to North Korea, working towards, in Lee’s words, “a Korean Peninsula where tensions are eased and coexistence is achieved through denuclearisation and peace.”

Yet Lee’s approach to North Korea is, in effect, a policy of unconditional appeasement. However well-intentioned, it has increasingly appeared ineffective or even counterproductive, undermining South Korea’s national security, failing to win Pyongyang over, and straining the United States-South Korea alliance.
Foundations of North Korea policy
The Lee Jae-myung government’s North Korea policy rests on three foundations.

First, it carries forward the vision of Kim Dae-jung, a founding figure of the Democratic Party and former South Korean president, who was awarded the 2000 Nobel Peace Prize in part “for his work . . . for peace and reconciliation with North Korea.”

Second, it appeals to the so-called National Liberation faction within the Democratic Party—Lee’s powerbase, whose members were active in the radical left-wing student movement of the 1980s and early 1990s and romanticised North Korea as the embodiment of national liberation and self-determination in the face of American imperialism.

Third, Lee’s “our North Korea” remarks as Democratic Party leader on 19 January 2024 suggest that his apparent sympathy for Pyongyang may be genuine rather than merely a form of political manoeuvring intended to compensate for his lack of involvement in the 1980s student movement. In those remarks, he stated, “Chairman Kim Jong-un should work hard to ensure that the efforts of his predecessors—our North Korea’s Kim Jong-il and President Kim Il-sung—are neither disparaged nor undermined.”
The evidence for characterising Lee’s North Korea policy as one of appeasement is reinforced by both the government’s words and actions.

Since July 2025, several Lee-appointed ministers have continued either to dispute the appropriateness of designating the North Korean regime and its military as South Korea’s “main enemy” or to sidestep the issue altogether. During the National Assembly’s Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee audit on 14 October 2025, Lee’s political mentor and Minister of Unification Chung Dong-young claimed, “It is me, Chung Dong-young, who understands President Lee Jae-myung’s conviction and philosophy better than anyone else… I believe the president does not consider North Korea the main enemy.” This flies in the face of Kim Jong-un’s 15 January 2024 declaration naming South Korea as his country’s “primary foe and invariable principal enemy.”

Then, frontline Republic of Korea (ROK) Army units were found to have performed “empty-gun guard duty” armed with either unloaded machine guns or expandable batons during the first half of 2026. This guard-duty rule was introduced by the ROK Army’s 1st Corps in January to prevent South Korean soldiers from accidentally firing towards North Korea, and later shared with the 2nd, 3rd, and 5th Corps.

More broadly, the Lee Jae-myung government’s overly conciliatory approach to North Korea may have created incentives for frontline ROK Army commanders to subordinate military necessity to political expediency. As an Army general asked rhetorically, “If the current administration were conservative, would the commander of the 1st Corps or the 25th Division have even imagined unloaded guns or batons?” This is hard to reconcile with North Korea’s continued efforts since 2024 to fortify the inter-Korean border within the demilitarised zone (DMZ) using landmines, barbed-wire fences, tactical roads, and anti-tank walls, with some of the 960,000 newly laid landmines injuring three South Korean military officers in the DMZ last September.
The failure of appeasement

Since Lee took office in June 2025 and began repeatedly calling for dialogue, North Korea has accelerated the expansion and operationalisation of its nuclear and conventional military capabilities, thereby posing an increasingly serious threat to South Korea’s national security.

North Korea has increased its nuclear arsenal to about 60 assembled warheads, with enough fissile material for at least 30 more, showing no sign of the nuclear freeze or reduction urged by Lee. Moreover, by upgrading its partnership with Russia and sending troops to fight in the war against Ukraine, North Korea has not only gained combat experience but also advanced its drone-warfare and missile capabilities. On 21 April, US Forces Korea Commander General Xavier T. Brunson told the US Senate Armed Services Committee that Russian-assisted advances in North Korea’s military capabilities represented “significant shifts,” not merely incremental gains.

Contrary to President Lee’s intentions, his appeasement policy has failed to win over Pyongyang, which has instead grown even more hostile towards Seoul. Notably, at a meeting with all division and brigade commanders in the North Korean army on 17 May, Kim Jong-un reportedly said, “Peaceful unification is out of the question, and we must settle accounts with South Korea by force”—a message subsequently relayed to troops across the North Korean armed forces through ideological education sessions.
The pacemaker and the peacemaker: Troubles in the US-South Korea alliance

Meanwhile, cracks have emerged in the US-South Korea alliance under Lee’s government. One major fault line concerns intelligence sharing on North Korea. Since April, the Trump administration has restricted intelligence sharing and cybersecurity cooperation with Seoul on North Korea, treating Minister of Unification Chung Dong-young’s public disclosure of classified information on a suspected North Korean uranium-enrichment facility in Kusong as a breach of trust and alliance standards. Washington has also reportedly complained about the decline in North Korea-related special intelligence from Seoul, because the Lee government’s post-martial-law restructuring and considerations about inter-Korean relations have weakened South Korea’s defence intelligence capabilities.

Another fault line lies in disagreement over South Korea’s proper role in US-North Korea diplomacy. Although Lee has cast himself as a “pacemaker” to Trump’s “peacemaker” since their first White House summit on 25 August 2025, Trump does not appear to take Lee’s role seriously. On 19 August, Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun indicated to the National Assembly’s Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee that Seoul had neither been briefed on the details of US-North Korea communications about a Trump-Kim meeting nor received a US response to its offer to serve as pacemaker.

On 24 August, Trump touted his relationship with Kim by posting three old photos of the two together on Truth Social without explanation—a gesture that left Lee out of the picture. Yet Lee, for his part, has blurred the line between pacemaker and peacemaker. In a New York Times interview published on 21 September, shortly before his United Nations General Assembly address and one month after calling for talks with Pyongyang to formally end the Korean War, Lee urged the US to ease sanctions on North Korea in exchange for a halt to further development of nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

As a former senior South Korean official wryly asked, “When Washington still holds fast to the principle of ‘the complete denuclearisation of North Korea,’ why is the ‘pacemaker’ (South Korea) trying to outpace the ‘real runner’ (the US)?” Indeed, on 27 October, Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun disclosed that during his meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio a month earlier, Washington had cautioned Seoul against “getting too far ahead” in its self-appointed pacemaker role.

Lee’s dialogue-oriented and conciliatory approach to North Korea marks a fundamental departure from that of his predecessor. He may well have pursued it with genuinely good intentions. Yet as a policy of unilateral, unconditional appeasement towards North Korea, it has increasingly appeared ineffective or even counterproductive. It is time for the Lee government to take stock of the policy’s actual consequences and to recalibrate its North Korea policy to the world as it is, not as Lee would wish it to be.
